vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: the independent organisation that checks the project and signs the credits
what a piece of land is used for: crops, cattle, forest or building
the document that shows, year after year, what the project actually did
the gases a company releases into the atmosphere
the place where credits are bought and sold, with a price
the level of emissions there would be without the project
the number above which the rule starts to apply to you
the proof that the reduction would not have happened anyway

items.situation: A manager asks: "Do we have to send the monitoring report every year?"
tips: Yes. Under the standard, we have to submit it every twelve months.
have to for a rule that comes from outside.

items.situation: He asks: "And can we choose the verification body ourselves?"
tips: We may choose it, but it must be accredited by the standard.
may for permission, must for the condition that limits it.

items.situation: He asks: "Can we clear the old trees to plant the new ones?"
tips: No, we cannot. Under the permit, existing forest must not be cleared.
cannot and must not are the two ways of saying it is forbidden.

items.situation: He asks: "Is it a problem if we start planting before the certification arrives?"
tips: It is not forbidden, but you should wait, because the baseline has to be measured first.
should when it is advice, not obligation.

items.situation: The finance director asks: "Might the price of a credit fall before we sell?"
tips: It might, because the carbon market moves with policy, not only with demand.
might for a real possibility that nobody controls.

items.situation: A colleague asks: "What does additionality mean, in one sentence?"
tips: It is the proof that the reduction would not have happened anyway.
No jargon. Say it the way you would to somebody outside legal.

listenings.text: Amanda, it is Bruno, the project manager in the north. I am on the site now and I have two questions that the team keeps asking me, and I do not want to answer them wrongly. First, the old trees at the edge of the area. They are not many and they are not healthy, and the planting crew says it would be faster to clear them. I told them to wait for you. Second, the timing. The certification people have not confirmed a date, and the rain starts in six weeks. If we wait for the certificate, we lose the season, and if we plant now, I do not know whether the credits still count. I am not asking you to guess. I am asking you to tell me what the rule says, and what you recommend. Call me when you can.

Welcome back. In this part of the session I want to talk about the three words that decide whether a project produces credits or produces nothing. The first is baseline. The baseline is the level of emissions there would be without the project, and everything you claim is measured against it, so if the baseline is wrong, every number after it is wrong too. The second is additionality. Additionality is the proof that the reduction would not have happened anyway, and it is the hardest one, because you are proving something about a world that does not exist. The third is monitoring. A project must report, year after year, what it actually did, and a verification body has to check it. And here is the part that surprises lawyers. None of these three is mainly a scientific question. All three are questions of evidence, and evidence is your job.

extra_audio.text: Start with what the rule obliges, using must or have to. Then say what it forbids, with cannot or must not. Then say what it allows, with may or can. Then say what you recommend, with should. And finally, say what might happen if the recommendation is ignored.
